function.name: cmd_controller_execute
function.description: Executes a system-level command using os.system() on Windows operating systems. It can execute single or multiple commands chained with '&&'. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

command.description: The system command to be executed. To execute multiple commands, separate them with '&&'. For example, 'dir && echo done'.

unit.description: Specifies the unit of measure for the command if applicable. This is not utilized by os.system() directly but can be used for logging or analysis purposes.

I don’t have a way to probe your connection from here, so I can’t tell you the exact speed right now. But you can quickly find out yourself with one of the following methods: | Method | How to do it | |--------|--------------| | **Web‑based speed test** | Open a browser and go to (or ). Click “Go” and wait for the test to finish. | | **Command‑line (Windows)** | If you have PowerShell, you can run a quick test with the `Test-NetConnection` cmdlet:
`Test-NetConnection -ComputerName www.google.com -Port 80`
This will give you latency and basic connectivity info, but not throughput. | | **Command‑line (Linux/macOS)** | Install `speedtest-cli` (Python package) and run:
`speedtest-cli --simple`
or just `speedtest` if you have the binary. | | **Mobile app** | Download the Speedtest app from Google Play or the App Store and run it. | If you want a more detailed report (latency, jitter, packet loss, etc.), the web site or the CLI tool will give you that. Once you run the test, you’ll see a download speed (Mbps), upload speed, and ping. That’s the best way to know your current internet speed.
